stats.line: About 1 in 3 daily smokers aged 18–25 met the doctors' checklist for weed addiction. Over 26, about 1 in 6 did.
stats.mirror: You're under 26, smoke almost every day, and wonder if it's a problem.

basis.who: people who used cannabis on 300 or more days in the past year
basis.n: 22,651 daily users across 2002–2016; the paper doesn't say how many were 18 to 25 in 2015–2016
basis.measured: whether their own answers met the older DSM-IV checklist for cannabis abuse or dependence in the past year

stats.caveat: Based on people's own answers and an older checklist. The share was higher in 2002–03 (about 45% at 18–25). It does not mean the rest have no problems.

ref.cite: Santaella-Tenorio J, Levy NS, Segura LE, et al. (2019). Cannabis use disorder among people using cannabis daily/almost daily in the United States, 2002–2016. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.

stats.line: Of Americans who used weed in the past month, 42% used it daily or almost daily. Among drinkers it was 11%.
stats.mirror: You smoke every day and call it how you relax.

basis.design: re-analysis of 27 national surveys (NSDUH and earlier versions)
basis.who: US general population aged 12 and over
basis.n: 1,641,041 people across 27 surveys; the summary doesn't say how many used weed in 2022
basis.measured: how many days in the past month people said they used cannabis or alcohol

stats.caveat: It counts days of use, not addiction. Many near-daily users have no disorder. Self-reported, US only.

ref.cite: Caulkins JP (2024). Changes in self-reported cannabis use in the United States from 1979 to 2022. Addiction.
ref.quote: In 2022, past-month cannabis consumers were almost four times as likely to report daily or near daily use (42.3% vs. 10.9%)

stats.line: Weed seized by US police in 2022 was about 4 times as strong as in 1995: about 16% THC instead of about 4%.
stats.mirror: You think it's the same weed your dad smoked.

basis.design: official lab testing program (NIDA Potency Monitoring Program, University of Mississippi)
basis.who: cannabis samples seized by the US Drug Enforcement Administration
basis.measured: average percent of THC, the part that gets you high, in seized cannabis

stats.caveat: Police seizures, not a random sample of what people smoke. Legal shop flower and concentrates can be stronger, over 40% THC.

ref.cite: National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA). Cannabis (Marijuana) research topic page, and Cannabis Potency Data, Potency Monitoring Program 1995–2022.
ref.quote: Between 1995 and 2022 the delta-9 THC potency (strength) in illegal cannabis products seized by law enforcement quadrupled from 3.96% to 16.14%.

stats.line: Adults who seek help for weed have smoked almost daily for over 10 years on average, and seriously tried to quit 6+ times.
stats.mirror: You've been meaning to cut down for years.

basis.design: review of US treatment research, summing up patient samples
basis.who: adults entering treatment for marijuana abuse or dependence
basis.n: The review sums up treatment studies, including ones with 229 and 450 adults
basis.measured: years of near-daily use and number of serious quit attempts before treatment, as patients reported

stats.caveat: Only people who sought treatment, who may be heavier users than most. It is an average, not a rule.

ref.cite: Budney AJ, Roffman R, Stephens RS, et al. (2007). Marijuana dependence and its treatment. Addiction Science & Clinical Practice.
ref.quote: Adults seeking treatment for marijuana abuse or dependence average more than 10 years of near-daily use and more than six serious attempts at quitting

stats.line: Of people who ever got hooked on weed, half got there within about 5 years of first using it.
stats.mirror: You started casually and slid into daily smoking over a few years.

basis.design: national survey, same people interviewed twice (NESARC)
basis.who: US adults who had ever used cannabis
basis.n: 529 people who became dependent (of 7,389 who had used weed)
basis.measured: years from first use to first meeting the older DSM-IV criteria for dependence

stats.caveat: Dependence here is the strict older definition. About 9% of users (8.9%) are projected to ever reach it, so most users never do.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Pérez de los Cobos J, Hasin DS, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of NESARC. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: Half of the cases of dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine were observed approximately 27, 13, 5 and 4 years after use onset, respectively.

stats.line: The chance of trying weed for the first time peaks at age 18. The chance of getting hooked peaks at 17–18 too.
stats.mirror: You started in your late teens and never really stopped.

basis.design: national survey (National Comorbidity Survey), survival analysis
basis.measured: age at first use, and age when people first met the criteria for dependence, from interviews

stats.caveat: Older data. It is the peak age, not the age everyone starts. Only about 8% of users became dependent within 10 years of first use.

ref.cite: Wagner FA, Anthony JC (2002). From first drug use to drug dependence; developmental periods of risk for dependence upon marijuana, cocaine, and alcohol. Neuropsychopharmacology.
ref.quote: With respect to risk of initiating use, estimated peak values for alcohol and marijuana were found at age 18

stats.line: Long-term users lost about 5.5 IQ points between childhood and age 45. People who never used held steady (+0.7).
stats.mirror: You've smoked for years and feel slower or more forgetful than before.

basis.n: 84 long-term users with IQ tests (of 1,037 in the study)
basis.measured: IQ at ages 7, 9, 11 and 45, plus memory and attention problems noticed by people who knew them

stats.caveat: Long-term means weekly use at 45 and at an earlier check-up; most had smoked 4+ days a week at some point. People who had quit by 45 had still dropped about 3 points. A link; tobacco, alcohol, other drugs and childhood class did not explain it.

ref.cite: Meier MH, Caspi A, Knodt AR, et al. (2022). Long-term cannabis use and cognitive reserves and hippocampal volume in midlife. American Journal of Psychiatry.
ref.quote: Their mean 5.5-point childhood-to-adulthood IQ decline was significantly larger than that observed among lifelong cannabis non-users (M=0.70)

stats.line: Of people raised middle class, 52% of those hooked on weed for years had dropped to a lower class than their parents by 38. Of non-users: 14%.
stats.mirror: You grew up comfortable, smoke heavily, and feel you're slipping behind.

basis.who: everyone born in Dunedin in one year (1972–73)
basis.n: 43 people hooked at 3 or more check-ups (of 947 studied); fewer of them grew up middle class, and the paper doesn't give that number
basis.when: followed from birth to age 38; cannabis asked about at 18–38
basis.measured: job and social class at 38 compared with their parents', among those raised middle class

stats.caveat: A small group, and a link, not proof. It held after allowing for childhood IQ, self-control, family history and other drugs. 'Hooked for years' means dependent at 3 or more check-ups between ages 18 and 38.

ref.cite: Cerdá M, Moffitt TE, Meier MH, et al. (2016). Persistent cannabis dependence and alcohol dependence represent risks for midlife economic and social problems: a longitudinal cohort study. Clinical Psychological Science.
ref.quote: "51.7% of formerly middle-class persistent cannabis users experienced downward mobility" versus "14.4% of Study members who never used cannabis."

stats.line: Smoking strong weed daily came with 4.8 times the odds of a first psychosis, losing touch with reality, versus never using.
stats.mirror: You smoke strong weed daily and have had paranoid or 'off' moments.

basis.who: people aged 18–64 with a first psychosis, and people from the same areas without it
basis.n: 901 people with a first psychosis and 1,237 without; the paper doesn't give how many of them smoked strong weed daily
basis.where: 11 sites in Europe and Brazil (e.g. London, Amsterdam)
basis.measured: how often people used cannabis and how strong it was (10% THC or more counted as strong)

stats.caveat: Odds, not risk: psychosis is rare, so most daily users never get it. It compares sick and healthy people, which cannot prove cause.

ref.cite: Di Forti M, Quattrone D, Freeman TP, et al. (2019). The contribution of cannabis use to variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across Europe (EU-GEI): a multicentre case-control study. Lancet Psychiatry.
ref.quote: increasing to nearly five-times increased odds for daily use of high-potency types of cannabis (4·8, 2·5-6·3)

stats.line: Men who smoked daily had about 4 times the odds of not being able to come during sex, compared with men who didn't use.
stats.mirror: You smoke daily and notice sex is harder to finish.

basis.who: Australians aged 16–64 living in homes with a landline
basis.n: 126 daily users, men and women together (of 8,656 surveyed); the paper doesn't say how many were men
basis.measured: self-reported sexual problems in the past year, such as not reaching orgasm or coming too fast

stats.caveat: Odds, not risk: it does not mean 4 times as many men. With so few daily users, the true figure could be anywhere from about 1.7× to 9×. A link, not proof of cause.

ref.cite: Smith AM, Ferris JA, Simpson JM, et al. (2010). Cannabis use and sexual health. Journal of Sexual Medicine.
ref.quote: daily use vs. no use was associated with increased reporting among men of an inability to reach orgasm (3.94, 1.71-9.07; P < 0.01)

stats.line: Withdrawal usually starts on day 1–3 and peaks on day 2–6. Most symptoms last 4–14 days.
stats.mirror: You're on day 3 off weed, angry and unable to sleep.

basis.design: 50-day outpatient study: 5 days of usual use, then 45 days off
basis.who: heavy marijuana users, plus ex-users for comparison
basis.measured: daily ratings of anger, anxiety, appetite, weight, irritability, restlessness, shakiness, sleep problems and stomach pain

stats.caveat: Small study of 18 people. These are typical times, and 'most' effects, not all. Your days can differ.

ref.cite: Budney AJ, Moore BA, Vandrey RG, Hughes JR (2003). The time course and significance of cannabis withdrawal. Journal of Abnormal Psychology.
ref.quote: Onset typically occurred between Days 1-3, peak effects between Days 2-6, and most effects lasted 4-14 days.

stats.line: 71% of people who got 2+ weeks off weed in treatment slipped at least once within 6 months, on average after about 73 days.
stats.mirror: You quit for a few weeks, then 'just had one'.

basis.design: follow-up of an outpatient treatment group
basis.who: adults in outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence who reached at least 2 weeks without weed
basis.measured: first use of any weed (a slip), and return to heavier use (4+ days in any 7 days), over 6 months

stats.caveat: Slips are common, not the end. But 71% of those who slipped went back to heavier use, and early slips were riskier. Small sample.

ref.cite: Moore BA, Budney AJ (2003). Relapse in outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment.
ref.quote: Seventy-one percent used marijuana at least once (i.e., lapsed) within 6 months of initial abstinence, averaging 73 days (SD = 50) till lapsing.

stats.line: Across 47 studies, 47% of regular or dependent weed users had withdrawal symptoms when they stopped.
stats.mirror: You got cranky and couldn't sleep the last time you stopped.

basis.who: people with regular cannabis use or cannabis use disorder; 69% men, median age about 30
basis.measured: share who met the criteria for cannabis withdrawal on a tested checklist

stats.caveat: It depends who is asked: 17% in general-population samples, 54% in outpatients, 87% in inpatients. Daily users had it more often.

ref.cite: Bahji A, Stephenson C, Tyo R, et al. (2020). Prevalence of cannabis withdrawal symptoms among people with regular or dependent use of cannabinoids: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Network Open.
ref.quote: The overall pooled prevalence of CWS was 47% (6469 of 23 518) (95% CI, 41%-52%)

stats.line: Only about 13% of Americans who ever had a weed addiction went to treatment or a 12-step group. Most never got formal help.
stats.mirror: You want to quit without rehab, therapy or meetings.

basis.n: 2,242 people who ever had a weed addiction (of 36,309 surveyed)
basis.measured: whether people who ever met the DSM-5 checklist for cannabis use disorder had ever used professional treatment or 12-step programs

stats.caveat: It shows most people never get help. It does not show how many of them quit on their own.

ref.cite: Hasin DS, Kerridge BT, Saha TD, et al. (2016). Prevalence and correlates of DSM-5 cannabis use disorder, 2012–2013: findings from NESARC-III. American Journal of Psychiatry.
ref.quote: Only 13.2% with lifetime cannabis use disorder participated in 12-step programs or professional treatment.

stats.line: In studies where users were off weed more than 72 hours, their test scores were no longer clearly worse than non-users'.
stats.mirror: You're afraid you've fried your brain for good.

basis.who: frequent or heavy cannabis users aged 26 or under (average 20.6, 68% male) vs people with little use
basis.n: 928 people in 15 studies that required 72+ hours off (of 69 studies in the review)
basis.measured: scores on memory, attention and other thinking tests

stats.caveat: Compares groups at one moment; it does not follow the same people. Young users only. Very long-term heavy users can still show drops (see the IQ study above).

ref.cite: Scott JC, Slomiak ST, Jones JD, et al. (2018). Association of cannabis with cognitive functioning in adolescents and young adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry.
ref.quote: studies requiring an abstinence period longer than 72 hours (15 studies; n = 928) had an overall effect size (d, -0.08 ...) that was not significantly different from 0

stats.line: Young regular users who stopped for a month got better at learning and remembering words, mostly in the first week.
stats.mirror: You feel foggy and forgetful and wonder if a month off helps.

basis.design: randomised study: 4 weeks off weed vs. carry on using
basis.who: regular users aged 16–25 from the community and a high school
basis.n: 62 asked to stop for a month vs 26 who kept using (55 stayed off all 30 days)
basis.measured: memory and attention tests at the start and every week for 4 weeks

stats.caveat: Memory improved; attention did not. Young users only. It could not say whether school or work results improved.

ref.cite: Schuster RM, Gilman J, Schoenfeld D, et al. (2018). One month of cannabis abstinence in adolescents and young adults is associated with improved memory. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry.
ref.quote: There was an effect of abstinence on verbal memory (P = .002) ... driven by improved verbal learning in the first week of abstinence.

stats.line: In a 12-week trial, people who cut down felt less anxious, less depressed and slept better than those whose use rose.
stats.mirror: You smoke to calm your nerves or to fall asleep.

basis.design: follow-up inside a 12-week medication trial (secondary analysis)
basis.who: adults aged 18–50 in a trial for cannabis use disorder
basis.measured: changes in anxiety, depression, sleep quality and quality of life, next to changes in weed use

stats.caveat: This is cutting down, not only quitting. Overall quality of life did not improve in 12 weeks. A link, not proof.

ref.cite: Hser YI, Mooney LJ, Huang D, et al. (2017). Reductions in cannabis use are associated with improvements in anxiety, depression, and sleep quality, but not quality of life. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment.
ref.quote: These results indicate a longitudinal relationship between reductions in cannabis use and improvements in anxiety, depression, and sleep quality.

rejected.claim: 20.6 million Americans had a marijuana use disorder in 2024; 64.2 million used in the past year (NSDUH 2024).
rejected.why: SAMHSA's site returned 403 to every fetch (curl, WebFetch, browser). Seen only in secondary sources, so not verified.

rejected.claim: About 3 in 10 people who use cannabis have cannabis use disorder (CDC facts page).
rejected.why: CDC page returned 403. The same idea is on the page already via Leung 2020 (22%); NIDA's page gives '22% to 30%'.

rejected.claim: 30.6% of US past-year users had a marijuana use disorder in 2012–13 (Hasin 2015, NESARC-III, n=36,309).
rejected.why: Verified, but left out: overlaps the Leung 22% figure already on the page and would clash with the daily-user figure from a different survey.

rejected.claim: Cannabis dependence remission about 17% per year (Calabria 2010 review).
rejected.why: Abstract gives only a 'conservative' rate for cannabis, from 3 studies with mixed definitions, and does not clearly say per year. Too unclear to show.

rejected.claim: Money: what a daily user spends per year.
rejected.why: No official or peer-reviewed source found with spending per user. Not computed from prices, since the rules forbid made-up numbers.

rejected.claim: Weekly (not daily) users: share who get hooked.
rejected.why: No separate figure found. Leung 2020's 33% for young weekly-or-daily users is already on the page.

rejected.claim: Recent users had 1.34× the odds of sleeping under 6 hours (Diep 2022, NHANES, US).
rejected.why: Verified, left out to stay at 14. Cross-sectional and modest. Can be added if a sleep stat is wanted.

rejected.claim: Brain cannabinoid receptors are about 20% lower in daily smokers and back to normal after about 4 weeks off (Hirvonen 2012, 30 men).
rejected.why: Verified (PubMed abstract plus PMC full text), left out to stay at 14. Good 'after' stat if a slot opens.

rejected.claim: 12.1% of frequent US users had withdrawal (Livne 2019, NESARC-III, n=1,527).
rejected.why: Verified, left out: next to the 47% figure it would confuse readers. The 47% caveat already notes 17% in general-population samples.

rejected.claim: Daily use before 17: 0.37 times the odds of finishing high school (Silins 2014).
rejected.why: Verified, left out: about teenagers, while readers are men in their 20s–30s.

rejected.claim: Dunedin persistent users lost about 8 IQ points (Meier 2012).
rejected.why: That number is not in the abstract fetched. Used Meier 2022 (−5.5 IQ points by age 45) instead. Note: Meier 2022 found quitters had still dropped 3.3 points, so the old line 'people who quit showed smaller or no drops' was wrong and was fixed.
